article.body:
Rafi Adler, olov hasholom, once told me something funny. “Sruli,” he said, “the world is such a small place, and news travels so fast, that when a man in Crown Heights sneezes, another man in Eretz Yisroel answers, ‘"G-d bless you."

How right he was. One second I was in Manhattan on mivtzoim and the next second, I was encircled by a group of news reporters clamoring to interview me. Who would imagine that just a few hours back I had received the sad news about the passing of my friend, the businessman, whom I visited every Friday? Who would believe that a kid my age was handed a $500,000 check? I felt dizzy and tired, let's not forget the Erev Shabbos factor, but something told me that this interview could be used to make a huge kiddush Hashem.

The reporters agreed to wait while I ran inside the house to consult with my parents. I explained to my parents, in brief, what had happened. I helped them get over their initial shock of the day’s events, got their okay to proceed with the interview, and ran back out to the crowd.

Then, scanning the group for the friendliest, most professional-looking reporter, I spotted a man with a notepad in his hand and a pencil behind his ear.

“Excuse me, sir,” I said to him confidently. Everyone’s heads turned to see who I had addressed. “Would you mind conducting the interview?”

“Great,” I replied. I invited all present to follow me into my dining room.

As the room filled up with the reporters, its elegant, Shabbos-like atmosphere was replaced with a tense mood. The silence was deafening.

“Ready when you are, Mr. Reporter,” I exclaimed. The initial dialogue focused on

the purpose of mivtzoim. “Who started mivtzoim?” the reporter asked.

the interview shifted to personal questions about my relationship with Rafi. Finally, the half-a-million-dollar question was asked: What was I going to do with all the money that I had just received?

Adults seem to undermine children’s ability to see beyond themselves. They think that kids spend money only on games and toys. I guess that is why the reporters’ mouths almost reached the floor as they listened to my response.

“In these envelopes,” I said, “I have a check for half a million dollars and a letter that Rafi Adler wrote to me. I would like to read to you a couple of lines from the letter.”

The world, Sruli, is filled with many empty vessels: people who spend their lives searching for ways to fill themselves up with things that will make them happy. I was so empty, Sruli. One day in my old age, I turned to G-d with a silent prayer. I asked Him to send me a sign that He cares about me, that I’m important to Him, and that I’m here for a reason. Two days later, your brother walked into my shop and asked if I was Jewish. You and your brother turned my life around. The stories and Torah thoughts that you shared with me awakened the Jew within me. All along, you never asked for a dime in return. I was overwhelmed by your sincerity and care. You gave of yourselves simply because I have a Jewish soul.

“Now, I’m just one boy who visited one man once a week,

but look at the difference I made in his life.” I continued. “Some of you may wonder how a kid like me finds enjoyment not only in sitting like a couch- potato at the computer, but in helping other Jews. The answer is my Rebbe, the Lubavitcher Rebbe. He believes that we children are the strongest muscle of the entire Jewish nation. When we learn Torah and do mitzvos, we bring peace and light into the world and ensure the well-being of our people.”

“The Rebbe organized an army for Jewish kids called ‘Tzivos Hashem’ which recognizes the power of children. This army is very special! We children are its soldiers and officers. The commander-in-chief is Hashem. We are sent on special missions to fight the Yetzer Hora, the evil inclination, and we help others do the same.”

“You all seem very curious as to what I plan to do with the money that I just received, right?”

“I would like to fulfill the Rebbe’s request that every effort be made to mobilize the ‘Army of Hashem. I would like to start a global recruitment campaign: signs, advertisements, whatever it takes. Children, everywhere, will be invited to join this wonderful army. Each and every Jewish boy and girl needs to be made aware of how powerful every Jewish child is. Jewish children could achieve the impossible by working together!”

“The rest of the money will fund thousands of Tzivos Hashem missions and rallies that will take place throughout the year. All in Mr. Adler olov hasholom’s memory!” The thought of doing something for Mr. Adler’s neshama made me feel a little better. I would definitely miss my friend.

Finally, the interview was over. My parents and I escorted the reporters out, closed the door, and quickly transformed the dining room into its previous Shabbosdik state.

When we got back into the living room, all three of us froze in our tracks. The friendly reporter who conducted the interview was still there. Trying to be polite, I said, “Thank you so much, sir, but we have to get ready for Shabbos now.”

“Okay,” I thought to myself, “this is getting weird.” Looking me in the eyes, the reporter stood up and in a soft voice said, “Allow me to formally introduce myself. My name is John Adler, Rafi Adler’s son.”
